entries.name: Maximum groundspeed
entries.evidence: (a) The groundspeed of the small unmanned aircraft may not exceed 87 knots (100 miles per hour).
entries.note: The single figure, both units as printed: 87 knots / 100 mph.

entries.name: Maximum altitude above ground level
entries.evidence: (b) The altitude of the small unmanned aircraft cannot be higher than 400 feet above ground level, unless the small unmanned aircraft: (1) Is flown within a 400-foot radius of a structure; and (2) Does not fly higher than 400 feet above the structure's immediate uppermost limit.
entries.note: 400 feet, and the 400-foot structure radius and 400-foot above-structure allowance as three distinct figures.

entries.name: Minimum flight visibility
entries.evidence: (c) The minimum flight visibility, as observed from the location of the control station must be no less than 3 statute miles. For purposes of this section, flight visibility means the average slant distance from the control station at which prominent unlighted objects may be seen and identified by day and prominent lighted objects may be seen and identified by night.
entries.note: 3 statute miles, plus the section's own definition of flight visibility, which is a definition and not a threshold. The figure is fixed and this entry states it, which is why it stays clear; the definition it quotes turns on 'prominent', which the corpus never fixes, and that is prominent-objects — carried by the entry that applies the definition rather than by the one that states the figure.

entries.name: Minimum distance from clouds
entries.evidence: (d) The minimum distance of the small unmanned aircraft from clouds must be no less than: (1) 500 feet below the cloud; and (2) 2,000 feet horizontally from the cloud.
entries.note: Both figures: 500 ft below, 2,000 ft horizontal. A single combined value would lose the distinction.

entries.name: Civil twilight, outside Alaska
entries.evidence: (1) Except for Alaska, a period of time that begins 30 minutes before official sunrise and ends at official sunrise; (2) Except for Alaska, a period of time that begins at official sunset and ends 30 minutes after official sunset;
entries.note: Both windows: 30 minutes before official sunrise to sunrise, and sunset to 30 minutes after.

entries.name: Groundspeed is within the limit
entries.evidence: (a) The groundspeed of the small unmanned aircraft may not exceed 87 knots (100 miles per hour).
entries.note: At, just below and just above 87 knots. The printed mph figure is a rounding of the knots figure; test which one governs.

entries.name: Altitude is within the limit
entries.evidence: (b) The altitude of the small unmanned aircraft cannot be higher than 400 feet above ground level, unless the small unmanned aircraft: (1) Is flown within a 400-foot radius of a structure; and (2) Does not fly higher than 400 feet above the structure's immediate uppermost limit.
entries.note: The plain 400 ft AGL case; inside a 400 ft radius of a structure; and the boundary where the aircraft is within the radius but above the structure's uppermost limit plus 400.

entries.name: Visibility and cloud clearance are met
entries.evidence: (c) The minimum flight visibility, as observed from the location of the control station must be no less than 3 statute miles. For purposes of this section, flight visibility means the average slant distance from the control station at which prominent unlighted objects may be seen and identified by day and prominent lighted objects may be seen and identified by night. (d) The minimum distance of the small unmanned aircraft from clouds must be no less than: (1) 500 feet below the cloud; and (2) 2,000 feet horizontally from the cloud.
entries.note: Each minimum independently, and the case where one passes and the other fails. The cloud-clearance half is fully computable from two stated figures. The visibility half is not: the quantity to be compared against 3 statute miles is the section's own 'flight visibility', whose definiens turns on which objects are 'prominent', and the corpus fixes no degree of prominence. That term is prominent-objects, split out rather than reclassifying this entry — classifying the whole entry by one of its clauses would have thrown away the 500-foot and 2,000-foot figures (0005).

entries.name: Which objects are prominent, for flight visibility
entries.evidence: For purposes of this section, flight visibility means the average slant distance from the control station at which prominent unlighted objects may be seen and identified by day and prominent lighted objects may be seen and identified by night.

ambiguity.question: Part 107 does not define 'prominent', and the term carries the whole visibility metric: the distance reported as flight visibility is the distance at which prominent objects can be seen, so the degree of prominence fixes the number that § 107.51(c)'s 3-statute-mile threshold is compared against.

entries.note: Gate 1 of 0008 passes: applying § 107.51(c) requires fixing a degree the corpus did not fix, which is what separates flight visibility from groundspeed — an ordinary caller-supplied parameter whose meaning is not open. Gate 2 does not fire: no corpus is named for it. Gate 3's first branch does not fire either — the clause states no measure for 'prominent' in its own constituent and names no decider — so the procedure returns a gap. The same shape as well-clear and moving-vehicle-operation's 'sparsely populated area'. Found by the undefined-term sweep (#33, #34), not by inspection of the interesting entries.

entries.name: Only one aircraft is operated at a time
entries.evidence: A person may not manipulate flight controls or act as a remote pilot in command or visual observer in the operation of more than one unmanned aircraft at the same time.
entries.note: One aircraft; two aircraft; and the same person acting as visual observer for a second. The prohibition binds three roles — manipulating the flight controls, acting as remote pilot in command, acting as visual observer — and the evidence covers each.

entries.name: Controlled airspace requires prior ATC authorization
entries.evidence: No person may operate a small unmanned aircraft in Class B, Class C, or Class D airspace or within the lateral boundaries of the surface area of Class E airspace designated for an airport unless that person has prior authorization from Air Traffic Control (ATC).
entries.note: Each of Class B, C, D and the lateral surface area of Class E, with and without authorization; and Class G, which needs none. The airspace class is an input. Determining it from a position requires a corpus this map has not admitted.

entries.name: Prohibited or restricted areas require permission
entries.evidence: No person may operate a small unmanned aircraft in prohibited or restricted areas unless that person has permission from the using or controlling agency, as appropriate.
entries.note: Both designations the section states — prohibited and restricted — with and without permission from the using or controlling agency. Same shape as airspace-authorized: the designation is an input, not something derived here.

entries.name: Operation from a moving vehicle or aircraft
entries.evidence: No person may operate a small unmanned aircraft system— (a) From a moving aircraft; or (b) From a moving land or water-borne vehicle unless the small unmanned aircraft is flown over a sparsely populated area and is not transporting another person's property for compensation or hire.

ambiguity.question: Part 107 does not define 'sparsely populated area', and the term carries the whole exception in (b).

entries.note: From a moving aircraft (always prohibited); from a moving land or water-borne vehicle over a sparsely populated area without carriage for hire; and the two ways the exception fails. The summary this note replaces said "a moving land vehicle" and dropped the water-borne case (#26).

entries.name: Operation at night
entries.evidence: (a) Except as provided in paragraph (d) of this section, no person may operate a small unmanned aircraft system at night unless— (1) The remote pilot in command of the small unmanned aircraft has completed an initial knowledge test or training, as applicable, under § 107.65 after April 6, 2021; and (2) The small unmanned aircraft has lighted anti-collision lighting visible for at least 3 statute miles that has a flash rate sufficient to avoid a collision. The remote pilot in command may reduce the intensity of, but may not extinguish, the anti-collision lighting if he or she determines that, because of operating conditions, it would be in the interest of safety to do so.

crossReferences.cites: Except as provided in paragraph (d) of this section
crossReferences.unmapped: § 107.29(d) is a transitional waiver-termination rule — after May 17, 2021 no night operation may be conducted under a certificate of waiver issued before April 21, 2021, and waivers issued before March 16, 2021 terminated on that date. It is spent, and this map's slice has no entry for it.

entries.note: Night with training and lighting; night without either; and the § 107.65 training date boundary of April 6, 2021. The training date and whether lighting is fitted are computable; the sufficiency of the flash rate is asserted (flash-rate-sufficient) and so is the pilot's safety determination (intensity-reduction-in-interest-of-safety), both reached through anti-collision-lighting, whose locator cites the clause that states them. But the condition of application is "at night", and § 107.3 does not define night — it defines seven terms and night is not among them. § 107.3 puts § 1.1 of this chapter in force for this part ("if there is a conflict… the definitions in this part control"), so gate 2 of 0008 routes the term to definedElsewhere rather than to a gap, and the whole entry declines: without the term no case of § 107.29(a) is reachable, not even the case where it does not apply. That is why this is not split the way civil-twilight-alaska is — there two of the three limbs of civil twilight are fixed in the section itself, and there is a passage stating the deferral; here no passage states what night means. The limit, stated where the claim is: § 107.3's clause is a general priority rule and does not route this term to § 1.1 by name, so the claim that § 1.1 fixes it becomes checkable only when cfr-14-1 is admitted. The "Except as provided in paragraph (d)" carve-out is a transitional waiver-termination rule, and this map has no entry for § 107.29(d).

entries.name: Operation during civil twilight
entries.evidence: (b) No person may operate a small unmanned aircraft system during periods of civil twilight unless the small unmanned aircraft has lighted anti-collision lighting visible for at least 3 statute miles that has a flash rate sufficient to avoid a collision. The remote pilot in command may reduce the intensity of, but may not extinguish, the anti-collision lighting if he or she determines that, because of operating conditions, it would be in the interest of safety to do so. (c) For purposes of paragraph (b) of this section, civil twilight refers to the following: (1) Except for Alaska, a period of time that begins 30 minutes before official sunrise and ends at official sunrise; (2) Except for Alaska, a period of time that begins at official sunset and ends 30 minutes after official sunset; and (3) In Alaska, the period of civil twilight as defined in the Air Almanac.
entries.note: Inside and outside each twilight window, with and without lighting. Alaska is a separate entry: the corpus defers the definition elsewhere.

entries.name: Civil twilight in Alaska
entries.evidence: (3) In Alaska, the period of civil twilight as defined in the Air Almanac.
entries.note: § 107.29(c)(3) fixes the meaning of Alaskan civil twilight in the Air Almanac, which this map has not admitted. Not an ambiguity: the corpus is clear, and the text that would settle it is elsewhere. Nothing beyond the quoted sentence can be evidenced from this corpus.

entries.name: Carriage of hazardous material
entries.evidence: A small unmanned aircraft may not carry hazardous material. For purposes of this section, the term hazardous material is defined in 49 CFR 171.8.
entries.note: § 107.36 states the prohibition here and fixes the meaning of 'hazardous material' in 49 CFR 171.8, which this map has not admitted. Not an ambiguity: the corpus says exactly what it means and says where. Nothing beyond the quoted sentences can be evidenced from this corpus.

entries.name: Yielding right of way to other aircraft
entries.evidence: (a) Each small unmanned aircraft must yield the right of way to all aircraft, airborne vehicles, and launch and reentry vehicles. Yielding the right of way means that the small unmanned aircraft must give way to the aircraft or vehicle and may not pass over, under, or ahead of it unless well clear.
entries.note: Two enumerations, both computable: three protected kinds — aircraft, airborne vehicles, launch and reentry vehicles — and three prohibited relative positions — over, under, ahead. An engine told the object is none of the three, or that the manoeuvre is none of the three, decides the case without the open term at all, and the evidence covers each. The note this replaces said "nothing here is computed", which its own evidence contradicts (#34). What is not computed is the exception "unless well clear", which is well-clear and is a gap rather than an assertion: 0008 § 2 attacked the purpose clause at this joint and it gave way, so gate 3's first branch does not fire here.

entries.name: The small unmanned aircraft is well clear of the aircraft or vehicle
entries.evidence: Yielding the right of way means that the small unmanned aircraft must give way to the aircraft or vehicle and may not pass over, under, or ahead of it unless well clear.

ambiguity.question: Part 107 does not define 'well clear', and the term carries the whole exception to the prohibition on passing over, under or ahead. 'Well clear' occurs exactly once in the corpus; § 107.3 does not define it and no other section does; and § 107.37(a) states no measure for it in its own constituent — 'must give way' is a coordinate obligation in the definiens, not what the clearance is measured against.

entries.note: Split out of right-of-way, which keeps the two computable enumerations (0005: a standard is its own entry, and the rule that consumes it depends on it). Not kind: assertion — gate 3's first branch requires the corpus to state, in the same constituent as the open term, either the measure or the set of values, and § 107.37(a) states neither. Not a value either: the corpus states no clearance. The kind records what the engine would have to do and cannot, which is why the entry declines at runtime rather than demanding a parameter. The same shape as moving-vehicle-operation's 'sparsely populated area', and the two now return the same answer, which they did not before. Where the project holds the term determinate — 'well clear' is a recognised operational standard in aviation practice — that is fate: decision with a record, never a kind (0008 § 3); this map does not hold it, so the fate is unresolved.

entries.name: Operating so close to another aircraft as to create a collision hazard
entries.evidence: (b) No person may operate a small unmanned aircraft so close to another aircraft as to create a collision hazard.
entries.note: The corpus states a standard rather than a distance, deliberately, and § 107.37(b) is that sentence and nothing else — so the entry is reclassified in place rather than split. The assertion is asserted and withheld, attributed and recorded with the outcome, and never defaulted to true when absent. An engine that resolved it to a number would substitute its own rule for the corpus's.

entries.name: A covered structure or stationary vehicle provides reasonable protection from a falling small unmanned aircraft
entries.evidence: (b) That human being is located under a covered structure or inside a stationary vehicle that can provide reasonable protection from a falling small unmanned aircraft
entries.note: The standard qualifies the covered-structure exception; the exception itself is computable once it is asserted. The assertion is asserted and withheld for each of a covered structure and a stationary vehicle, attributed and recorded with the outcome, and never defaulted to true when absent. Split out rather than reclassifying over-human-beings, which states two further cases that need no judgement.

entries.name: Operation over a human being
entries.evidence: No person may operate a small unmanned aircraft over a human being unless— (a) That human being is directly participating in the operation of the small unmanned aircraft; (b) That human being is located under a covered structure or inside a stationary vehicle that can provide reasonable protection from a falling small unmanned aircraft; or (c) The operation meets the requirements of at least one of the operational categories specified in subpart D of this part.
entries.note: Two causes, two entries. The judgement in (b) is reasonable-protection, an assertion. The deferral in (c) is subpart-d-categories, which is scope: out and carries OutsideCurrentScope itself — a dependency, not a second reason on this entry. The evidence is the whole section: the participating-person case, both limbs of (b) — a covered structure and a stationary vehicle — and the subpart D case, plus a plain overflight with none of them.

entries.name: Operational categories for flight over human beings
entries.evidence: This subpart prescribes the eligibility and operating requirements for civil small unmanned aircraft to operate over human beings or over moving vehicles in the United States, in addition to those operations permitted by § 107.39(a) and (b).
entries.note: Out of scope for this trial, which maps subpart B only. Reachable from § 107.39(c), so an engine must be able to say OutsideCurrentScope rather than simply lacking it. Nothing under the subpart is worked; the evidence is the subpart's own applicability sentence, which is what makes the citation checkable at all.

entries.name: The anti-collision lighting has a flash rate sufficient to avoid a collision
entries.evidence: (2) The small unmanned aircraft has lighted anti-collision lighting visible for at least 3 statute miles that has a flash rate sufficient to avoid a collision. ... (b) No person may operate a small unmanned aircraft system during periods of civil twilight unless the small unmanned aircraft has lighted anti-collision lighting visible for at least 3 statute miles that has a flash rate sufficient to avoid a collision.
entries.note: The same clause qualifies the night requirement in (a)(2) and the civil-twilight requirement in (b), which is why it hangs off anti-collision-lighting — the entry whose locator cites both — rather than off night-operation alone. The assertion is asserted and withheld, attributed and recorded with the outcome, and never defaulted to true when absent; the corpus states no rate, so no figure is evidenced. Added by Amendment 107-8; the 2020 text states no flash-rate requirement anywhere.

entries.name: Reducing the anti-collision lighting intensity is in the interest of safety
entries.evidence: The remote pilot in command may reduce the intensity of, but may not extinguish, the anti-collision lighting if he or she determines that, because of operating conditions, it would be in the interest of safety to do so.
entries.note: The corpus delegates the judgement and names its decider in the same breath: "if he or she determines". § 107.29(a)(2) and (b) state the identical sentence, which is why the locator cites both and why the quoted evidence has two occurrences. The computable half stays where it was: the bound that intensity may be reduced but the lighting may not be extinguished is anti-collision-lighting's, and that entry depends on this one — the speed-limit / speed-within-limit shape 0005 names. This is the example method.md and corpus-map.md both cite for kind: assertion, and it had no entry of its own until #26.

entries.name: Anti-collision lighting is fitted and visible for 3 statute miles
entries.evidence: (2) The small unmanned aircraft has lighted anti-collision lighting visible for at least 3 statute miles that has a flash rate sufficient to avoid a collision. The remote pilot in command may reduce the intensity of, but may not extinguish, the anti-collision lighting if he or she determines that, because of operating conditions, it would be in the interest of safety to do so. ... (b) No person may operate a small unmanned aircraft system during periods of civil twilight unless the small unmanned aircraft has lighted anti-collision lighting visible for at least 3 statute miles that has a flash rate sufficient to avoid a collision. The remote pilot in command may reduce the intensity of, but may not extinguish, the anti-collision lighting if he or she determines that, because of operating conditions, it would be in the interest of safety to do so.
entries.note: Fitted and unfitted, for night and for civil twilight; the 3 statute mile visibility figure the corpus states plainly; and the bound the same clause states — the intensity may be reduced but the lighting may not be extinguished. Whether reducing it is in the interest of safety is the remote pilot in command's determination and is its own entry, intensity-reduction-in-interest-of-safety; the sufficiency of the flash rate is flash-rate-sufficient.

entries.name: Visual line of sight is maintained
entries.evidence: (a) With vision that is unaided by any device other than corrective lenses, the remote pilot in command, the visual observer (if one is used), and the person manipulating the flight control of the small unmanned aircraft system must be able to see the unmanned aircraft throughout the entire flight in order to: (1) Know the unmanned aircraft's location; (2) Determine the unmanned aircraft's attitude, altitude, and direction of flight; (3) Observe the airspace for other air traffic or hazards; and (4) Determine that the unmanned aircraft does not endanger the life or property of another. (b) Throughout the entire flight of the small unmanned aircraft, the ability described in paragraph (a) of this section must be exercised by either: (1) The remote pilot in command and the person manipulating the flight controls of the small unmanned aircraft system; or (2) A visual observer.
entries.note: Whether anyone could in fact see the aircraft is not computable. The engine demands the assertion and records who made it. (b) states the two permitted combinations and the evidence covers both: the remote pilot in command together with the person manipulating the flight controls, or a visual observer — and neither.

entries.name: Visual observer requirements, when one is used
entries.evidence: If a visual observer is used during the aircraft operation, all of the following requirements must be met: (a) The remote pilot in command, the person manipulating the flight controls of the small unmanned aircraft system, and the visual observer must maintain effective communication with each other at all times. (b) The remote pilot in command must ensure that the visual observer is able to see the unmanned aircraft in the manner specified in § 107.31. (c) The remote pilot in command, the person manipulating the flight controls of the small unmanned aircraft system, and the visual observer must coordinate to do the following: (1) Scan the airspace where the small unmanned aircraft is operating for any potential collision hazard; and (2) Maintain awareness of the position of the small unmanned aircraft through direct visual observation.
entries.note: All three requirements, not just the first: effective communication at all times, the remote pilot in command ensuring the observer can see the aircraft in the manner § 107.31 specifies, and the coordination (c) requires. With and without a visual observer, and with one whose communication requirement is unmet.

entries.name: Preflight familiarization, inspection and actions
entries.evidence: Prior to flight, the remote pilot in command must: (a) Assess the operating environment, considering risks to persons and property in the immediate vicinity both on the surface and in the air. This assessment must include: (1) Local weather conditions; (2) Local airspace and any flight restrictions; (3) The location of persons and property on the surface; and (4) Other ground hazards. (b) Ensure that all persons directly participating in the small unmanned aircraft operation are informed about the operating conditions, emergency procedures, contingency procedures, roles and responsibilities, and potential hazards; (c) Ensure that all control links between ground control station and the small unmanned aircraft are working properly; (d) If the small unmanned aircraft is powered, ensure that there is enough available power for the small unmanned aircraft system to operate for the intended operational time; (e) Ensure that any object attached or carried by the small unmanned aircraft is secure and does not adversely affect the flight characteristics or controllability of the aircraft; and (f) If the operation will be conducted over human beings under subpart D of this part, ensure that the aircraft meets the requirements of § 107.110, § 107.120(a), § 107.130(a), or § 107.140, as applicable.
entries.note: Six obligations, all assertions about what a person did. The engine records them; it cannot verify any. Each of (a) through (f) asserted and unasserted; (f) is reachable only through subpart D.
